title: Off Broadway Review: CABLE STREET - Bored and Confused?

Now, Cable Street is inspired by a real historical event from October 1936 when residents of Cable Street in London's East End, Jewish immigrants, Irish immigrants, English working class locals, dock workers, communists, all of them banded together and barricaded their street to stop a fascist parade. Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists, the Blackshirts, had been given permission to march through this primarily Jewish neighborhood, and tens of thousands of people on the ground refused to let it happen. In the show, we have one main character pulled from each of those communities. We have Sammy Scheinberg, a young Jewish would-be boxer played by Isaac Green, Mairead Casey, a young Irish woman who wants to be a poet working in a Jewish bakery played by Lizzie Rose Essen Kelly, and Ron Williams, a young Englishman who can't get work and is feeling lost played by Barney Wilkinson. The story follows their three lives, their relationships with their families, and how the rise of this fascist movement in Britain pulls them together. Ron, the unemployed Englishman, gets drawn in by the Blackshirts who tell him that immigrants are the reason he can't get a job. Sammy can't get hired because he's Jewish and there's anti-Semitism everywhere he turns. The Irish family is barely making rent just like everyone else. There's also a framing device, a contemporary American woman comes to East London to take a walking tour of the Cable Street area hoping to reconnect with her late mother. The tour becomes our doorway into the 1930s. Let's start with positives. This is a very ambitious show and it's done with a small ensemble of about 13 actors, each playing at least three roles. They play all the Jewish residents, all the Irish residents, all the English residents, the fascists, and the communists, and the police. Considering how confusing it could be, the actors are very clear with their dialects and the director, Adam Lenson, does a great job moving this ensemble around a very small space. I was really impressed at how clear the narrative was despite these limitations of the space and the size of the company. My hat is off to the director and the cast. They're fully committed and they're very skilled. I have to commend the show, too, for being timely. It's directly addressing the fascist movement of the 1930s and the way those in power and those with wealth turn poor immigrants and poor English locals against each other in order to maintain control. It also has elements of the greedy upper class squeezing every cent out of these poor people. And all of it lands. Why this style for this character? When the rap started, I went, "Oh, no. Are we going to be doing Hamilton for the whole show?" Fortunately, no. It's just Sammy who's stuck in Hamilton.
